Let’s talk about something we all face— change.
Chapter 7: Embracing Change—Impermanence and the Art of Letting Go.
Change is one of those things that’s always around the corner... and honestly, it might be the only real constant in life. But isn’t it funny how hard it can be to accept? We hang on to our routines, our relationships, even our sense of who we are, almost as if we could hold back the tide.
But in Taoist thinking, change isn’t something to fear. It’s the very fabric of existence—a kind of dance, filled with arrivals and departures, ups and downs, that gives our lives meaning and depth. Picture a couple who’s been married for decades. Suddenly, retirement is here. The habits and patterns that shaped their lives start to fade away, and with them, a sense of certainty. There’s some grief there, sure. But beneath it, there’s this quiet excitement—a chance to rediscover themselves, and each other.
Even in all that uncertainty, they stumble on moments of unexpected joy: a walk together at sunset, picking up a new hobby, or just having a deeper conversation than before. By letting go of what was, they find space for something beautiful and new. Most of us don’t realize just how much suffering comes from fighting change. Our minds cling to what’s familiar, worried about loss and the unknown. But Taoism invites us to look at impermanence differently—to see change as natural, maybe even beautiful. Think of the seasons shifting, or the moon cycling through its phases. Everything in life is always moving. The more tightly we hold on, the more we set ourselves up for frustration and sorrow. There’s also the story of a teacher, watching her students graduate. She feels a tug of sadness—the classroom will be quieter, her days a bit emptier. But as she lets go, she discovers a new sense of freedom. There’s room to explore, to rest, and to grow in ways she hadn’t imagined. The loss is real, but so is the possibility that follows. Letting go isn’t about being cold or detached. It’s about meeting each moment as it comes—allowing things to arrive and depart without clinging or pushing away. Most folks don’t realize it, but this kind of openness is actually a source of strength. It’s how we stay resilient, and move through life with a bit more grace. In Taoist tradition, impermanence isn’t a problem to solve—it’s a reality to embrace. The more we can let go, the more fully we get to live. The world feels less scary, and every moment—no matter how brief—starts to feel like a gift. Unique, fleeting, and truly precious.
